exact_edit_log.section: 1. Convertir el tiempo de guerra en normalidad
exact_edit_log.old: Aquí importa, sobre todo, que ese cuerpo no se desmontó cuando terminó la contienda, como había ocurrido después de la Primera Guerra Mundial. Recordemos el ensayo 17. Al acabar aquella guerra, Estados Unidos se apresuró a volver a la normalidad y redujo considerablemente la maquinaria estatal de tiempos de guerra. Esta vez sucedió lo contrario. El cuerpo administrativo que había crecido durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial no se encogió; la Guerra Fría lo fijó en su sitio, en nombre de la seguridad nacional, y lo convirtió en la normalidad de los siguientes cincuenta años.
exact_edit_log.new: Aquí importa, sobre todo, distinguir la desmovilización de la permanencia de una arquitectura de seguridad. Recordemos el ensayo 17. Al acabar la Primera Guerra Mundial, Estados Unidos se apresuró a volver a la normalidad y redujo considerablemente la maquinaria estatal de tiempos de guerra. Después de 1945 también hubo una gran reducción de efectivos y gastos militares. Pero esa reducción no impidió que la Guerra Fría consolidara, en nombre de la seguridad nacional, un entramado permanente de instituciones y preparación estratégica que marcaría los siguientes cincuenta años.
exact_edit_log.reason: Distinguish postwar demobilization from enduring security architecture.

exact_edit_log.section: 3. Los cimientos institucionales del Estado de seguridad nacional
exact_edit_log.old: En los ensayos anteriores, cada ampliación del Estado administrativo iba todavía acompañada de la expectativa de que algún día se revertiría. La fundación del Estado de seguridad nacional convirtió por primera vez esa ampliación en una estructura permanente que no se pensaba desmontar. Por primera vez en la historia de esta construcción, el poder ejecutivo quedó fijado en el centro del orden constitucional bajo una forma semipermanente.
exact_edit_log.new: En los ensayos anteriores, las ampliaciones ligadas a una emergencia iban acompañadas de la expectativa de que algún día retrocederían, aunque también dejaran instituciones duraderas. La fundación del Estado de seguridad nacional dio a esa capacidad ampliada una nueva arquitectura permanente que no se pensaba desmontar al terminar una crisis concreta. El poder ejecutivo adquirió así una posición central y semipermanente en la organización de la seguridad nacional.
exact_edit_log.reason: Preserve thesis without denying durable earlier institutions.

exact_edit_log.section: 3. Los cimientos institucionales del Estado de seguridad nacional
exact_edit_log.old: Por grandes que fueran, todas esas expansiones seguían atadas a una crisis concreta que acabaría pasando. Al menos cabía esperar que, una vez superada, el poder ampliado volviera a reducirse. La fundación del Estado de seguridad nacional rompió por primera vez esa expectativa.
exact_edit_log.new: Por grandes que fueran, esas expansiones se justificaban por circunstancias concretas que acabarían pasando, aunque no todos sus efectos fueran reversibles. Al menos cabía esperar que, una vez superadas, parte del poder ampliado volviera a reducirse. La fundación del Estado de seguridad nacional debilitó esa expectativa en el ámbito de la seguridad.
exact_edit_log.reason: Calibrate absolute first/permanence framing.

exact_edit_log.section: IV. Johnson y la reescritura de las reglas
exact_edit_log.old: Prohibió pruebas como las de alfabetización y otros procedimientos de ese tipo, y estableció, en las jurisdicciones sujetas a la ley, funcionarios federales encargados de examinar las solicitudes de inscripción electoral y un mecanismo de autorización previa.
exact_edit_log.new: Suspendió pruebas como las de alfabetización y otros procedimientos de ese tipo en las jurisdicciones cubiertas por la fórmula legal, donde también dispuso la intervención de examinadores federales y un mecanismo de autorización previa.
exact_edit_log.reason: 1965 suspension initially applied to covered jurisdictions.

exact_edit_log.section: V. Por qué esta inclusión duró más que la de la Reconstrucción
exact_edit_log.old: La protección federal durante la Reconstrucción dependía, en el fondo, de una voluntad política: de que el Norte quisiera seguir comprometiendo recursos, de que el Gobierno federal quisiera mantener sus tropas. Cuando esa voluntad se agotó, la protección se desmoronó con ella. La ley de 1965 hizo algo distinto. En vez de confiar en que el Gobierno federal mantuviera indefinidamente su disposición política, adelantó la supervisión al momento anterior a cualquier cambio de reglas, mediante la autorización previa de su sección 5.
exact_edit_log.new: La protección federal durante la Reconstrucción tenía bases constitucionales y legales, pero su aplicación dependía mucho de que el Norte siguiera comprometiendo recursos y el Gobierno federal mantuviera la protección efectiva. Cuando esa voluntad se agotó, la protección se desmoronó. La ley de 1965 introdujo un mecanismo distinto: mediante la autorización previa de su sección 5, adelantó la supervisión al momento anterior a los cambios de reglas en las jurisdicciones cubiertas. No eliminó la necesidad de ejecución ni de apoyo político y judicial, pero redujo la dependencia de una nueva decisión federal ante cada maniobra discriminatoria.
exact_edit_log.reason: Reconstruction had law; preclearance was not independent of enforcement.

exact_edit_log.section: IX. Conclusión
exact_edit_log.old: Si esta reescritura duró más que la Reconstrucción, fue porque transformó la inclusión: de promesa frágil, dependiente de la voluntad política, pasó a ser un conjunto de reglas exigibles encajadas en la maquinaria legal.
exact_edit_log.new: Si esta reescritura duró más que la Reconstrucción, fue en parte porque reforzó la inclusión mediante mecanismos de aplicación más estables. No convirtió una mera promesa en derecho por primera vez, ni dejó de necesitar voluntad política: redujo la dependencia de intervenciones federales decididas caso por caso.
exact_edit_log.reason: Keep durability thesis without automatic enforcement.

exact_edit_log.reason: Distinguish approximate inherited force from announced target.

exact_edit_log.section: V. Watergate y la corrección repartida entre muchos
exact_edit_log.old: La sentencia fijó un principio constitucional más amplio: el presidente no dispone de un privilegio ejecutivo que le permita bloquear de forma absoluta un requerimiento judicial de pruebas en materia penal.
exact_edit_log.new: La sentencia rechazó así un privilegio absoluto basado en una invocación general de confidencialidad frente a aquel requerimiento penal, sin negar toda protección a las comunicaciones presidenciales.
exact_edit_log.reason: Bound Nixon holding to generalized confidentiality.

exact_edit_log.section: VIII. El caso Irán-Contra y la persistencia de los excesos del ejecutivo
exact_edit_log.old: Ni la Comisión Tower ni la investigación conjunta del Congreso desembocaron en una conclusión tan simple como la existencia de un plan delictivo explícito en la cúspide de la Casa Blanca. Ambas, sin embargo, formularon críticas severas contra el funcionamiento del Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, la pérdida de control sobre los procedimientos, el desorden de los registros y la cadena de responsabilidades.
exact_edit_log.new: No se demostró que Reagan hubiera conocido de antemano el desvío de fondos, pero eso no equivalía a que no hubiera actuaciones ilegales ni responsabilidades en los niveles superiores del gobierno. La Comisión Tower y la investigación conjunta del Congreso formularon críticas severas contra el funcionamiento del Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, la pérdida de control sobre los procedimientos, el desorden de los registros y la cadena de responsabilidades.
exact_edit_log.reason: Separate unproven prior knowledge from wrongdoing and responsibility.

exact_edit_log.section: VII. La dureza y el giro de los últimos años de la Guerra Fría

exact_edit_log.new: El tratado exigía eliminar los misiles balísticos y de crucero de base terrestre con alcances de entre 500 y 5.500 kilómetros y sus lanzadores, tanto si llevaban cargas nucleares como convencionales. exact_edit_log.section: 3. La guerra del Golfo y el nuevo orden mundial
exact_edit_log.old: La guerra del Golfo mostró, de manera poco habitual, otra posibilidad: una guerra limitada, con autorización internacional, objetivos claros y voluntad de contención. Bush encuadró por iniciativa propia el poder presidencial de hacer la guerra en un marco de alianzas, objetivos y plazos. Pero esa autolimitación era una elección, no una garantía. Dependía del juicio del presidente, no de una imposición de las instituciones.
exact_edit_log.new: La guerra del Golfo mostró, de manera poco habitual, otra posibilidad: una guerra limitada, con autorización internacional, autorización del Congreso en enero de 1991, objetivos claros y voluntad de contención. Bush encuadró el poder presidencial de hacer la guerra en un marco de alianzas, objetivos y plazos. La decisión de no ampliar la guerra dependió también de su juicio, pero no operó en un vacío institucional: hubo autorizaciones y límites políticos concretos. Esa combinación no garantizaba que los presidentes futuros mantuvieran la misma contención.
exact_edit_log.reason: Add congressional authorization; distinguish personal restraint from absence of institutional constraints.

exact_edit_log.section: 4. Los problemas internos de Bush padre y las elecciones de 1992
exact_edit_log.old: Con ella, las personas con discapacidad, un grupo largamente desatendido en la vida pública, pasaron a contar por primera vez con un marco federal integral de derechos civiles que las protegía sistemáticamente contra la discriminación.
exact_edit_log.new: Con ella se amplió de forma decisiva la protección federal contra la discriminación de las personas con discapacidad, un grupo largamente desatendido en la vida pública. No partía de cero: la sección 504 de la Ley de Rehabilitación de 1973 ya había establecido una protección importante en programas con financiación federal.
exact_edit_log.reason: ADA built on existing Section 504 protections.

exact_edit_log.section: 7. La globalización, la nueva economía y los restos internos
exact_edit_log.old: Por un lado, el Tratado de Libre Comercio de América del Norte, la Organización Mundial del Comercio, las relaciones comerciales normales permanentes con China y la revolución de internet impulsaron realmente el comercio, la inversión, la integración de las cadenas de suministro, el aumento de la productividad y la mejora del bienestar de los consumidores. Por otro, el mismo proceso produjo dentro de Estados Unidos pérdidas muy concentradas y difíciles de reparar por sí solas.
exact_edit_log.new: Por un lado, el Tratado de Libre Comercio de América del Norte, la Organización Mundial del Comercio y la revolución de internet impulsaron realmente el comercio, la inversión, la integración de las cadenas de suministro, el aumento de la productividad y la mejora del bienestar de los consumidores. Las relaciones comerciales normales permanentes con China profundizarían después esa integración. Por otro, a lo largo de ese proceso, tanto en los años noventa como en su prolongación posterior, se produjeron dentro de Estados Unidos pérdidas muy concentradas y difíciles de reparar por sí solas.
exact_edit_log.reason: Do not attribute later PNTR effects to the 1990s; retain gains/costs argument.

exact_edit_log.section: V. Por qué esta inclusión duró más que la de la Reconstrucción
exact_edit_log.old: Ahí está la diferencia fundamental entre una inclusión duradera y una frágil. La primera ancla los derechos del resto en los engranajes de las instituciones; la segunda se limita a colgarlos de la veleta política.

Esos engranajes también necesitan mantenimiento, pero hacen más difícil deshacer una victoria.

PATCO refusal to return and distinct legal regime; quarter-specific public-debt series; full INF missile/launcher scope; Iran-Contra prior-knowledge finding distinguished from wrongdoing and presidential responsibility.

shared_calibrations.debt_numbers: Original 24.8/39.1 values retained after root verified FRED FYGFGDQ188S (1981Q1 24.76392; 1989Q4 39.06522). Final quarter explicitly falls in George H. W. Bush's presidency.

ep21.en.old: The previous essay closed with the observation that the man who inherited the wartime state in a matter of hours would preside over its transformation from hot war to cold — cementing the national security apparatus forged in combat into something approaching permanent infrastructure.
ep21.en.new: The man who inherited the wartime state in a matter of hours would preside over its transformation from hot war to cold — reorganizing its security capabilities into something approaching permanent infrastructure.

ep21.en.old: not merely the beginning of the Cold War, but the moment when wartime administrative expansion stopped being temporary.
ep21.en.new: not merely the beginning of the Cold War, but the consolidation of a lasting national-security architecture out of wartime expansion.

ep21.en.old: This time there was no dismantling. The Cold War provided something unprecedented: a crisis without foreseeable end. Every previous administrative expansion in this series was tethered to a particular emergency — a civil war, a depression, a world war — with the implicit expectation of eventual retraction. The Cold War severed that tether. The permanent reason for emergency was born.
ep21.en.new: After 1945, too, there was large-scale demobilization and a sharp reduction in military spending. Yet the Cold War supplied a crisis without foreseeable end around which core security capabilities could be reorganized into lasting institutions. Earlier expansions had also left enduring agencies, but their emergency powers were justified by particular crises — a civil war, a depression, a world war — with some expectation of eventual retraction. In national security, the Cold War weakened that expectation. A durable reason for emergency was born.
ep21.en.reason: Acknowledge postwar demobilization and prior permanent agencies.

ep21.en.old: NSC-68 then provided the ideological spine — rejecting both isolationism and accommodation in favor of sustained, globally calibrated military and industrial buildup.
ep21.en.new: NSC-68 then provided the ideological spine — weighing continuation of existing policies, isolationism, and war against a rapid buildup of the free world's political, economic, and military strength, and favoring the last course.

ep21.en.old: Previous administrative expansions in this series had always carried the expectation of eventual contraction; crises had ends, and governments were supposed to return to normalcy. The national security state inverted this logic. Its justifying crisis was structural and indefinite. The administrative expansion it produced was thus, for the first time, designed never to be reversed.
ep21.en.new: The New Deal had already left lasting administrative institutions; permanence itself was not new. What changed was the organization of wartime security powers around a crisis understood as structural and indefinite. These capabilities were no longer expected to disappear at the end of a particular war. The national security state gave them a new, semi-permanent institutional form.

ep21.en.old: This is the deepest difference from all earlier expansions.
ep21.en.new: This marks a new stage in the organization of national-security power.
ep21.en.reason: Avoid absolute contrast with all earlier expansion.

ep21.en.old: Truman framed the intervention as a United Nations police action, thus bypassing the constitutional requirement for formal authorization. This was not semantics: it established the template that every subsequent president would draw on when committing American forces to sustained combat abroad.
ep21.en.new: Truman framed the intervention as a United Nations police action without seeking a congressional declaration or specific statutory authorization, setting off an enduring constitutional dispute. This was not merely semantics: it established an influential postwar template for committing American forces to sustained combat abroad.
ep21.en.reason: State contested authorization issue without declaring settled law or universal subsequent use.

ep21.en.old: Every debate about Vietnam, Lebanon, Grenada, and beyond would circle back to this founding instance of undeclared major war.
ep21.en.new: Later debates about Vietnam, Lebanon, Grenada, and beyond would repeatedly return to this major postwar precedent for war without a declaration.
ep21.en.reason: Postwar precedent, not first undeclared war.

ep21.en.old: the national security state's core institution would be the first venue for desegregation
ep21.en.new: the national security state's core institution would become an important early venue for postwar federal desegregation

ep21.en.old: Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 did not merely reverse Plessy; it articulated what Harlan's solitary dissent had maintained for half a century — that the Constitution is color-blind, that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. The seed planted in Harlan's dissent, buried in the legal record through the Jim Crow decades, had germinated. The Supreme Court retrieved a promise the Constitution had made and then abandoned.
ep21.en.new: Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 rejected separate-but-equal in public education, holding that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. For this series, the decision recalls the promise defended in Harlan's solitary dissent in Plessy, though Brown's reasoning was not simply a restatement of his color-blind Constitution. The seed planted in that dissent, buried in the legal record through the Jim Crow decades, had germinated. The Supreme Court returned to an equality promise that Plessy had betrayed.
ep21.en.reason: Separate Brown holding from Harlan's dissent and retain interpretive continuity.

ep21.en.old: The CIA could overthrow a foreign government without congressional debate, public knowledge, or any mechanism of regular review.
ep21.en.new: The CIA could help overthrow a foreign government without public congressional debate or public knowledge, while secret oversight remained limited and concentrated in a few hands.
ep21.en.reason: Bound deficient accountability rather than denying any oversight.

ep22.en.old: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 broke a Senate filibuster — the longest in Senate history to that point — by a vote of seventy-one to twenty-nine, with a coalition of forty-four Democrats and twenty-seven Republicans.
ep22.en.new: The Senate ended the prolonged filibuster against the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by a vote of seventy-one to twenty-nine, with a coalition of forty-four Democrats and twenty-seven Republicans.
ep22.en.reason: Identify Senate cloture action and avoid overly broad longest-ever claim.

ep22.en.old: It eliminated literacy tests and similar devices and, crucially, established a preclearance system under Section 5 requiring jurisdictions with a history of discrimination to obtain federal approval before changing any election rule.
ep22.en.new: It suspended literacy tests and similar devices in jurisdictions covered by its statutory formula and, crucially, established a preclearance system under Section 5 requiring those jurisdictions to obtain federal approval before changing any election rule.
ep22.en.reason: Initial test suspension and preclearance coverage.

ep22.en.old: Alabama's Black voter registration rose from 19.3 percent before the Voting Rights Act to 51.6 percent afterward.
ep22.en.new: In Alabama, voter registration among the predominantly Black population classified as non-white in the statistical table rose from 19.3 percent before the Voting Rights Act to 51.6 percent afterward.
ep22.en.reason: Identify CRS table category without changing numbers.

ep22.en.old: The Fifteenth Amendment was constitutional in form and sweeping in aspiration, but it made federal protection contingent on sustained federal political will. When that will withdrew — when Northern voters tired of Reconstruction, when troops were pulled — the amendment became a dead letter.
ep22.en.new: Reconstruction had constitutional and statutory protections, but their enforcement depended heavily on sustained federal political will. When that will withdrew — when Northern voters tired of Reconstruction, when troops were pulled — those guarantees could be hollowed out.
ep22.en.reason: Reconstruction had enforceable laws, not only aspirational promise.

ep22.en.old: Southern jurisdictions could not implement new electoral procedures without federal approval. The monitoring was automatic, not discretionary. Durable inclusion depends on anchoring rights in institutional machinery, not in the goodwill of the moment. This is the distinction between inclusion that holds and inclusion that doesn't.
ep22.en.new: Covered jurisdictions could not implement new electoral procedures without federal approval. This reduced dependence on a fresh federal response to each discriminatory maneuver; it did not eliminate the need for enforcement or political and judicial support. Durable inclusion requires rights to be anchored in the machinery of everyday enforcement, not merely proclaimed. That machinery still needs maintenance, but it makes a victory harder to reverse.
ep22.en.reason: Preclearance was proactive but not independent of politics, courts and implementation.

ep22.en.old: The Watts uprising in 1965 lasted six days, killed thirty-four, injured more than a thousand, and arrested nearly four thousand.
ep22.en.new: The Watts uprising in 1965 lasted six days and left thirty-four dead, more than a thousand injured, and nearly four thousand under arrest.

ep22.en.old: The year closed with his assassination, Robert Kennedy's assassination, and the chaos of the Chicago Democratic convention — a fracture without clean resolution.
ep22.en.new: The year's sequence of shocks included his assassination, Robert Kennedy's assassination, and the chaos of the Chicago Democratic convention — a fracture without clean resolution.
ep22.en.reason: Assassinations in April/June, not end of year.

ep22.en.old: The reversal was more durable than Reconstruction because it lodged in self-executing institutional mechanisms rather than in temporary political will.
ep22.en.new: The reversal proved more durable than Reconstruction in part because its enforcement mechanisms reduced dependence on repeated, case-by-case political decisions, while still requiring sustained support.

ep23.en.old: the story of how the long line of administrative expansion crested and was finally broken.
ep23.en.new: the story of how the long line of administrative expansion crested and met a powerful institutional check.
ep23.en.reason: Avoid final permanent defeat contradicted by essay's ending.

ep23.en.old: The problem was not one man's character; it was a body that had been fed for a century and finally found a master willing to use its full strength.
ep23.en.new: The problem was not only one man's character; it was also a body that had been fed for a century and finally found a master willing to use its full strength. The structural explanation does not diminish Nixon's personal responsibility.
ep23.en.reason: Structural explanation is not personal absolution.

ep23.en.old: was not a mandate. It was a coalition
ep23.en.new: was not a landslide popular mandate. It was a coalition
ep23.en.reason: Distinguish narrow victory from no electoral mandate.

ep23.en.old: Nixon inherited 550,000 American troops in Vietnam and reduced that number to 69,000 by 1972. American combat deaths fell from 16,899 in 1968 to 68 in 1973.
ep23.en.new: Nixon inherited roughly half a million American troops in Vietnam and announced in January 1972 a target of reducing that number to 69,000. American military deaths fell from 16,899 in 1968 to 68 in 1973.
ep23.en.reason: Approximate inherited strength, announced target, and deaths not all battle deaths.

ep23.en.old: The crime was not the break-in but the cover-up:
ep23.en.new: The scandal was not only the break-in but also the cover-up:

ep23.en.old: unanimous Supreme Court rejection of absolute executive privilege, establishing that no president stands above criminal judicial process.
ep23.en.new: unanimous Supreme Court rejection of an absolute privilege based on a generalized claim of confidentiality against the criminal subpoena, without denying all protection to presidential communications.

ep23.en.old: Remove any of those contingencies and the outcome changes.
ep23.en.new: Remove one of those contingencies and the outcome might have changed.

ep23.en.old: Ford's accession was itself a constitutional novelty — the first president who had attained both the vice presidency and the presidency through appointment rather than election, under the Twenty-Fifth Amendment.
ep23.en.new: Ford's accession was itself a constitutional novelty: he became vice president through nomination and congressional confirmation under the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, then succeeded automatically to the presidency when Nixon resigned, without having been elected to either office.
ep23.en.reason: Distinguish appointment/confirmation as VP from automatic presidential succession.

ep23.en.old: required congressional notification within forty-eight hours of committing troops to hostilities and mandated withdrawal within sixty days absent formal authorization.
ep23.en.new: required congressional notification within forty-eight hours of committing troops to hostilities and generally required termination within sixty days of the report being submitted or becoming due, absent a declaration of war, specific authorization, or congressional extension; it allowed up to thirty additional days when specified military conditions required time for safe withdrawal.
ep23.en.reason: Reporting clock and conditional 30-day withdrawal extension.

ep24.en.new: He negotiated the Panama Canal's eventual transfer to Panama.
ep24.en.reason: Distinguish treaty negotiation from completed handover; retain explicit Canal antecedent.

ep24.en.old: The credit for taming inflation belongs to both administrations. The political costs fell disproportionately on Carter.
ep24.en.new: The Federal Reserve under Volcker led the anti-inflation effort across both administrations. Carter paid a heavy political price for the crisis, while the deep 1981–82 recession also imposed major costs during Reagan's presidency.
ep24.en.reason: Preserve independent Fed role and cross-presidency costs.

ep24.en.old: Reagan's offer — restored confidence, morning in America, no apologies —
ep24.en.new: Reagan's offer — restored confidence, national renewal, no apologies —
ep24.en.reason: Avoid placing the 1984 campaign phrase in 1980.

ep24.en.old: Reagan's 1981 inaugural declaration — "government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem" —
ep24.en.new: Reagan's 1981 inaugural declaration — "In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem" —
ep24.en.reason: Restore contextual opening of quoted statement.

ep24.en.old: The national debt held by the public grew from approximately 24.8 percent of GDP at the start of 1981 to roughly 39.1 percent by the end of 1989.
ep24.en.new: Federal debt held by the public grew from approximately 24.8 percent of GDP in the first quarter of 1981 to roughly 39.1 percent in the fourth quarter of 1989, by then during George H. W. Bush's presidency.
ep24.en.reason: Verified FRED quarters; latter observation is after Reagan left office.

ep24.en.old: Reagan's dismissal of striking air traffic controllers signaled that the federal government would no longer function as the natural protector of organized labor.
ep24.en.new: Reagan's dismissal of air traffic controllers who refused to return to work signaled that the federal government would no longer function as the natural protector of organized labor. These were federal employees subject to a statutory strike ban, not private-sector workers covered by the Wagner Act.
ep24.en.reason: Preserve symbolic reversal while clarifying distinct legal regimes.

ep24.en.old: the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty did eliminate an entire class of nuclear weapons — the first such agreement in Cold War history.
ep24.en.new: the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty required elimination of ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometers and their launchers, whether nuclear- or conventionally armed — a Cold War breakthrough in removing an entire class of missile systems rather than merely capping numbers.

ep24.en.old: The Tower Board and congressional investigations found no evidence of a criminal command structure comparable to Watergate's.
ep24.en.new: The Tower Board and congressional investigations did not establish that Reagan knew in advance about the diversion of funds. That did not exonerate senior officials or erase the serious deception and illegality the investigations exposed. They sharply criticized the NSC's operations, lost procedural control, confused records, and chain of responsibility; the congressional report placed ultimate responsibility on the president.
ep24.en.reason: No proven prior presidential knowledge is not absence of wrongdoing; retain findings and responsibility.

ep25.en.old: The previous essay ended by noting that a seasoned diplomatic president would preside over the Cold War's peaceful end and a quick military victory, followed by a younger successor who would declare a new prosperity in a unipolar moment — an era when many began speaking of the end of history.
ep25.en.new: A seasoned diplomatic president would preside over the Cold War's peaceful end and a quick military victory, followed by a younger successor who would declare a new prosperity in a unipolar moment — an era when many began speaking of the end of history.

ep25.en.old: German unification on October 3, 1990, and Soviet dissolution on December 25, 1991 completed the sequence.
ep25.en.new: German unification on October 3, 1990, Gorbachev's resignation on December 25, 1991, and the Soviet Union's formal dissolution the following day completed the sequence.

ep25.en.old: The Gulf War demonstrated the alternative: international authorization, explicit objective, self-imposed termination when the objective was met. Bush voluntarily framed presidential war-making within multilateral constraints. This was a choice, not an institutional requirement — which is precisely why it proved difficult to reproduce.
ep25.en.new: The Gulf War demonstrated an alternative: international authorization, congressional authorization in January 1991, an explicit objective, and termination when that objective was met. Bush framed presidential war-making within multilateral constraints and a statutory authorization tied to the UN resolutions. His judgment still mattered, as did pressure from other institutions and allies. This combination of legal limits and personal restraint was not a guarantee that every later president would reproduce it.
ep25.en.reason: Add congressional authorization; no purely personal restraint outside institutional constraints.

ep25.en.old: Disabled Americans had been largely invisible in the formal civil rights framework; the ADA placed them within it.
ep25.en.new: The ADA greatly widened federal protections for disabled Americans, building on earlier guarantees such as Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.
ep25.en.reason: Avoid ignoring existing disability rights law.

ep25.en.old: NAFTA, effective January 1, 1994; the WTO; China's Permanent Normal Trade Relations status; the internet revolution — these produced real gains in productivity, trade integration, and consumer welfare.
ep25.en.new: NAFTA, effective January 1, 1994; the WTO; the internet revolution — these produced real gains in productivity, trade integration, and consumer welfare. Legislation approving Permanent Normal Trade Relations with China in 2000 laid groundwork for further integration afterward; its later effects should not be projected back onto the 1990s boom.
ep25.en.reason: PNTR's later implementation/effects were not a 1990s cause.

ep25.en.old: prompted withdrawal within days and shaped subsequent risk calculus.
ep25.en.new: prompted an announcement of withdrawal within days and shaped subsequent risk calculus.
ep25.en.reason: Distinguish announced withdrawal from completed withdrawal.

ep25.en.old: The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling on December 12 — holding that Florida's use of different recount standards across counties violated equal protection, and that no constitutional recount could be completed within the statutory deadline — ended the dispute by judicial decree.
ep25.en.new: The Supreme Court ended Florida's recount on December 12. Seven justices found constitutional problems with the existing recount arrangements, but they divided over the remedy. A five-justice majority, interpreting Florida law as requiring adherence to the federal safe-harbor deadline, concluded that a constitutional recount could not be completed in time. The 5-4 division concerned ending this recount, not a general federal prohibition on counting after that deadline.
ep25.en.reason: Separate constitutional finding from disputed remedy and safe-harbor interpretation.

ep25.en.old: a 5-4 Supreme Court decision that half the country did not accept.
ep25.en.new: a 5-4 Supreme Court decision that many Americans continued to contest.
ep25.en.reason: Avoid unsupported numerical claim and distinguish contestation from refusal to accept peaceful outcome.
